newsitem.title: USA: U.S. troops to stay in Bosnia until March.
newsitem.headline: U.S. troops to stay in Bosnia until March.

text.p: Some 5,000 U.S. troops will begin moving into Bosnia within days to help cover the withdrawal of 52,000 international peacekeepers this year and stay on in Bosnia until March, the Pentagon said on Tuesday.
March would be more than two months after the mission of the current NATO-led military peace implementation force (IFOR), which includes 15,800 U.S. soldiers, ends on Dec. 20.
"It (the cover force) is scheduled to depart in March," Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters.

"I would expect in the next couple of days," he said in response to questions on when the U.S. protective force would start moving into Bosnia from Germany. He said he expected the movement order to be signed this week.

Bacon stressed that NATO and the United States had made no decision on whether a follow-on force to IFOR would be sent to Bosnia next year to keep peace in the country, saying that the cover force was only to provide security for removal of IFOR troops.
Most of the current force will remain in Bosnia until municipal elections are held there in November and then begin a rapid drawdown, which is expected to end in January.
"The coming (cover) force will remain after IFOR goes" until March, Bacon said. "It will go in and perform security functions after IFOR packs up and goes."
President Bill Clinton stressed repeatedly that all U.S. troops would be out of Bosnia on or shortly after the December 20 deadline for IFOR.

Defence Secretary Willian Perry and other NATO defence ministers at a meeting in Bergen, Norway, last week ordered alliance military officials to begin drawing up sets of contingency plans for a possible "post-IFOR" peacekeeoing force in troubled Bosnia next year.
Officials of several other allied nations said they were prepared to commit troops to a new force but would not do so unless the United States took part.
The issue could be politically explosive ahead of the U.S. presidential elections in early November.

Republican Senator Strom Thurmond of South Carolina, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, complained on Tuesday that Perry declined an invitation to testify on Bosnia before the committee on Wednesday.

"They (the Clinton administration) said that the mission would be completed by December. Maybe they need to come back to Congress for another authorisation," said committee member John McCain, an Arizona Reublican.

But Bacon told reporters that Perry had scheduling conflicts on Wednesday and that the secretary was keeping his schedule flexible in case he was called to play a role in Mideast summit talks in Washington.

"The secretary has talked with the committee about coming up and (privately) briefing members of the committee. He also has been talking to members on the phone about last week's meeting of the NATO ministerial meeting at which the subject of Bosnia arose," Bacon said.

The spokesman appeared to suggest that the time would not come to testify publicly about Bosnia options until they are prepared in detail. He said he did not expect such details until late October or perhaps the middle of November.
"We will definitely consult with Congress at the appropriate time," Bacon told reporters.
But Thurmond warned Perry in a letter that his decision not to testify Tuesday might hurt administration efforts to win Congress's approval if it decides to send U.S. troops back to Bosnia.

"You and President Clinton may find that it will be difficult for this committee, the Congress and indeed the American people to support any follow-on efforts in Bosnia when members of the administration cannot find the time to fully and openly explain their policies," Thurmond wrote.
